stem:
Tom, aged 12, is brought to his GP because his parents think his puberty has begun. For about a year he has had body odour and a few fine hairs at the base of the penis. He has grown steadily along the 25th centile with no recent acceleration. On examination, both testes measure 2 mL with an orchidometer.

Which is the correct interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Puberty has begun, as pubic hair is its first sign in boys
options.explanation: Pubic hair and body odour are driven by adrenal as well as testicular androgens, so they can appear with adrenarche before true puberty. They do not define its onset.

options.label: B
options.text: Puberty is delayed for his age and needs investigating now
options.explanation: Puberty in boys is delayed only if there is no testicular enlargement by 14 years. At 12, prepubertal testes are still normal.

options.label: C
options.text: Central puberty has not begun, as the testes are under 4 mL
options.explanation: Testicular enlargement to 4 mL or more marks the onset of central puberty in boys, normally between 9 and 14 years. At 2 mL, his hair and odour reflect adrenarche, and central puberty has not yet begun.

options.label: D
options.text: Puberty is precocious, as hair appeared before he turned 12
options.explanation: Precocious puberty in boys means signs before 9 years. Fine pubic hair at 11-12 is within the normal range, and his testes are prepubertal.

options.label: E
options.text: Puberty has begun but stalled, as his growth has not sped up
options.explanation: Boys have their growth spurt late in puberty, well after testicular enlargement begins, so no acceleration yet is expected rather than a sign of stalling.

context: Puberty in boys starts with testicular volume of 4 mL or more, normally at 9-14 years. Enlargement before 9 is precocious; none by 14 is delayed.
